    RECENT — Therapy Notes Addendum: Somatic Experience, Sensory Exploration & Emotional Regulation

    1. I think I have always experienced the world through my senses

    Something I realized recently is that I may be naturally very drawn to sensory experiences.

    When I think about my childhood in West End, Tortola, I remember spending hours exploring my outside environment.

    I would touch things, collect things, watch insects, explore plants, play with water, observe things, and listen to the sounds around me.

    Sometimes I would sit on the couch and listen to the ocean while watching cars pass by.

    I could do this for hours without becoming bored.

    I wasn’t necessarily looking for something to do. I was content observing, listening, touching, and experiencing my surroundings.

    I remember being happy alone.

    I think this is important because I don’t want to interpret every desire for solitude or sensory stimulation as a response to trauma.

    I genuinely enjoyed exploring the world.

    I wonder whether sensory exploration has always been one of the ways I experience pleasure, curiosity, and connection with my environment.

    2. The water experience helped me recognize something about myself

    Recently, when I was experiencing intense emotions, I spent time with water.

    I wasn’t simply putting my hands in it. I repeatedly glided my fingers through the water in a rhythmic motion.

    I noticed the sensation of my fingers moving through it, the resistance, and how weightless my fingers began to feel.

    The more I repeated the movement, the more absorbed I became.

    It felt like the weight was melting away.

    I described it as:

    “Every time I glided my fingers, I felt how weightless my fingers became, and then it didn’t feel like I had a care in the world. I kind of just got lost.”

    I think two things happened simultaneously:

    • My anger became less intense or disappeared.
    • The sensory experience became so interesting and pleasurable that my attention was absorbed in it.

    But there was another feeling.

    It reminded me of being a child again, alone and exploring my outside environment, happy simply experiencing life.

    I wasn’t thinking about responsibilities, relationships, or what anyone needed from me.

    I was just experiencing something.

    3. Why I want to understand my somatic experience

    I notice that physical experiences can sometimes reach me in ways that thinking, explaining, or talking don’t.

    When I’m emotionally overwhelmed, I can experience intense physical urges. I may want to move, hit something, break something, or withdraw.

    But the water experience showed me that physical sensation doesn’t have to be destructive.

    My body can also experience pleasure, curiosity, rhythm, movement, and relief.

    I want to understand why I seem to respond so strongly to sensory experiences.

    Some possibilities I want to explore include:

    • Whether childhood stress influenced how my nervous system responds to emotions.
    • Whether I had fewer opportunities to experience co-regulation and learned to manage distress independently.
    • Whether I naturally have strong sensory interests or preferences.
    • Whether repetitive movement and predictable sensory feedback help me regulate.
    • Whether physical experiences give me a sense of autonomy that interpersonal interactions sometimes don’t.
    • Whether I have always used sensory exploration as a way to experience pleasure and engage with the world.

    I don’t want to assume trauma explains everything. I want to understand both my learned responses and my natural sensory preferences.

    4. I want to distinguish different experiences

    I want to understand the difference between:

    • Dissociation: Staring into space, with my mind completely blank.
    • Sensory absorption: Becoming deeply interested in a physical sensation or movement.
    • Regulation: Experiencing a shift in emotional or physical intensity.
    • Pleasure: Enjoying an experience simply because it feels good.
    • Exploration: Engaging with my environment out of curiosity.
    • Freedom: Experiencing myself without feeling responsible for managing everything around me.

    The water experience felt like sensory absorption, pleasure, and relief. It also reminded me of childhood exploration.

    I don’t want to confuse that with the blankness I experience when I dissociate.

    5. What I want to explore

    I want to develop a better understanding of the sensory experiences that feel natural and satisfying to me.

    I want to explore:

    • Water and repetitive hand movements.
    • The sound of running water and the ocean.
    • Repetitive rhythms and tapping.
    • Music, humming, and singing.
    • Dancing and swaying.
    • Walking and observing my surroundings.
    • Touching different textures.
    • Exploring nature, plants, stones, and other objects.
    • Watching movement in my environment.
    • Combining music, movement, and journaling.

    I want to discover what I enjoy when I am not trying to solve a problem.

    I want to have more opportunities to experience life rather than constantly manage it.

    My Somatic Guide: what I can do when my emotions become intense

    This is not a list of things I have to complete. It is a collection of physical experiences I can explore when I feel overwhelmed, angry, restless, disconnected, or emotionally overloaded.

    The goal is not to force myself to calm down.

    The goal is to give myself another way to experience what is happening in my body.

    First: Notice what kind of experience I need

    When I feel physically restless:

    • Sway from side to side.
    • Walk around at a comfortable pace.
    • Shift my weight between my feet.
    • Roll my shoulders.
    • Dance to a song.
    • Repeat a simple movement until it feels satisfying.

    When I feel angry or physically tense:

    • Glide my hands through shallow water.
    • Press my palms together and slowly release.
    • Push gently against a wall.
    • Squeeze and release a soft towel or cushion.
    • Try slow, deliberate arm movements.
    • Walk while allowing my body to move naturally.

    I want to give physical energy somewhere safe to go without hitting myself, another person, or objects.

    When I feel overwhelmed by thoughts:

    • Listen to running water.
    • Listen to the ocean or nature sounds.
    • Hum a familiar melody.
    • Focus on one repeated physical movement.
    • Watch something moving, such as water, leaves, or passing cars.
    • Sit somewhere comfortable and observe my surroundings.

    When I feel disconnected or blank:

    • Notice the temperature of the room.
    • Feel my feet against the floor.
    • Touch a familiar textured object.
    • Describe five things I can see.
    • Listen to a familiar song.
    • Try gentle movement and notice whether I feel more connected afterward.

    I don’t have to force myself out of dissociation. I can gently orient myself to the present and seek support if I remain disconnected or unsafe.

    My sensory exploration menu

    Water

    • Glide my fingers through water.
    • Trace circles with my fingertips.
    • Move my palms back and forth.
    • Let water run over my hands.
    • Listen to the sound of water moving.

    Movement

    • Sway.
    • Dance.
    • Walk.
    • Shift my weight.
    • Move my arms in repeated patterns.
    • Stretch gently.

    Sound

    • Listen to the ocean.
    • Listen to running water.
    • Hum.
    • Sing.
    • Listen to music with a steady rhythm.
    • Experiment with repeating a musical phrase.

    Touch

    • Explore soft fabrics.
    • Run my fingers over smooth stones.
    • Touch leaves and plants.
    • Hold a textured object.
    • Explore different sensations without needing to accomplish anything.

    Observation

    • Watch cars passing.
    • Watch leaves moving.
    • Observe insects.
    • Look at the movement of water.
    • Sit outside and listen to the environment.

    I want to remember that observation itself can be an activity. I don’t have to be doing something productive to be engaged with life.

    A small routine for intense emotional moments

    When I notice my emotions becoming physically intense:

    • Pause. I don’t have to act on the first physical urge.
    • Notice. What am I experiencing physically? Tension, restlessness, heat, pressure, or an urge to move?
    • Choose. What kind of sensory experience sounds appealing right now?
    • Explore. Try one movement or sensation without demanding that it work.
    • Notice the change. Am I feeling less tense, more present, more absorbed, or simply different?
    • Decide what I need next. I can continue, change activities, take space, or seek support.

    I don’t have to make the feeling disappear immediately.

    If an urge to hurt myself or someone else becomes difficult to control, I need to create distance from anything I could use to cause harm and reach out for immediate support.

    My personal observations

    What sensations feel most satisfying to me?

    What movements do I naturally repeat?

    What sounds help me become absorbed?

    What physical experiences make me feel lighter?

    What do I enjoy even when I am not upset?

    What helps me feel present when I am disconnected?

    What changes in my body after a sensory experience?

    A reminder to myself

    I don’t have to wait until I’m overwhelmed to experience my body.

    I can explore because I’m curious.

    I can move because movement feels good.

    I can listen because I enjoy the sound.

    I can touch, observe, sing, dance, and experience my environment without turning everything into a task.

    I don’t have to be productive to deserve an experience.

    Sometimes I can simply sit, listen to the ocean, watch the world move, and be alive in it.

    I want to make room for that part of myself again.

    RECENT — friendships: what keeps bothering me, and what I want to work out

    • The cycle I keep seeing: I give a lot, say plainly when something hurts (my version of whispering), get little back, build up, snap — and then they pull away. Their pulling away confirms what I already believe: I'm fine without them and they're fine without me.
    • My role: the mom friend and confidante. People tell me things they don't tell their own therapists. I absorbed it all, carried it home with nowhere to put it, and it came out on my family — so I withdrew. It isn't a punishment; it's moving a limited amount of energy to my kids, my partner and myself.
    • What I gave versus what I got: I gave a safe space while pregnant when a friend was in a bad way, set up accounts so friends could fund their GoFundMes, and bought plane tickets. In return: no help when I asked for formula money, then a holiday other people had paid up front for; outfit pictures I asked for that never arrived; hearts instead of replies; warmth in public comments and silence in private.
    • Carl was happy to take my fully paid-off iPhone to bring on a trip with Q, Race and the girlfriend who doesn't like me. I didn't give it to her. This is the clearest example of why I feel used: she'll accept what I give while keeping me out of the circle it's travelling into.
    • Carl only came to me for her emotional needs. She lets other people do things for her: Q dyes her hair the same colour it has been for years, and she has a job but never sat down to apply for insurance so she could see a therapist.     RECENT — my mom: the dream realization that laid the craving to rest

    I've been sitting with something that I think finally closes a question I've been circling in here for weeks: whether I still, underneath everything, crave a relationship with my mom.

    • I tried to connect with her many times over the years, specifically by sharing my dreams with her. In Obeah tradition, dreams carry real spiritual weight — they can be messages, warnings, visitations. She knows this; it's part of where we're both from.
    • Every time I brought her a dream, she never engaged with it, never showed real interest, never asked a follow-up question. Not once, across many attempts.
    • Remembering that pattern clearly — not just the big disclosures and betrayals, but this smaller, repeated, specific thing — is what let the craving actually rest. This wasn't me giving up on hoping. This was me testing it, honestly, more than once, with something that mattered to me and to our shared culture, and getting a clear, consistent answer.
    • I think this is different from the earlier grief work ("I wanted a mom, not necessarily my mom"). That was about the role. This is about her specifically — proof that even on the terms most likely to reach her (something spiritual, something from home), she wasn't going to meet me. I don't think I'm waiting on anything from her anymore.

    Anger during caregiving (already discussed with Leah)

    • Caring for my daughter keeps bringing up repetitive, no-relief moments that spike into real anger — it's escalated to punching the bathroom mirror, breaking my laundry basket. I have a new cut or injury some days.
    • 5-senses grounding doesn't work for this and makes it worse — I'm not disconnected, I'm overloaded. Adding more sensory input into an already heightened state isn't the right tool.

    • The real question underneath it: why isn't anything I do enough? Why can't I just help her? Reflux often genuinely can't be fixed by doing everything right — it's not a competence problem. But it's landing on top of a lifetime of giving everything to people and having it not be enough or not be reciprocated, so hitting something that truly can't be fixed by effort isn't registering as just this one frustration — it's colliding with the oldest fear I have, that no matter how much I give or how well I do everything, it still won't be enough.
    • Anger might be the only emotion that gets through when I'm overstimulated, not the only one I feel — a flooded system doesn't have bandwidth to sort exhaustion, helplessness, or fear into separate lanes, so it collapses into the one channel that was always loud enough to be heard. Worth exploring with Leah: not "why don't I feel other things," but "why has anger always been the only door."

    Why I'm bringing this

    I know what's happened. What I want from these sessions is the why — how these patterns actually formed and how they're still showing up in my life now, especially at home. Two sessions in, still getting to know each other, so I want to give you the fuller picture at once instead of piecing it together over months, since I know part of how you work is researching theories that connect to what a client brings you and sharing them back. I wanted to give you enough material up front to actually do that.

    Pattern 1 — Connecting back to the anger/regulation question I asked last session

    You already have the Walmart replacement-item spiral from last session, so I won't re-walk it — just flagging it here because it belongs in the same throughline as everything above: I extend real care and attention to matching what someone actually wants (like I would have with the shopping substitution), and I don't handle it well when that same care isn't extended back to me.

    This connects to the hyperindependence — I don't handle disappointment well, especially when it involves someone not extending the care I would extend to them.

    Why my thoughts feel personified / poetic

    This came up when you asked me to explain it and I realized I don't actually have language for it beyond "you know what I mean" — so here's an actual attempt.

    • I grew up essentially alone. My mom parentified me, and intellectually she wasn't able to help me even when she tried — she was studying for her HHA certification and would have meltdowns because she couldn't retain the material, repeated things constantly, never remembered. So I taught myself everything I know, on my own, from very young.
    • In the absence of other people, my imagination had an enormous amount of uninterrupted time to grow. There was no one to talk to, so my inner world became the place things got worked out — and it grew fluid and poetic because it had to fill the role other people would normally fill.
    • That's where the personification comes from — it's not decoration, it's structural. My mind built its own internal company to make up for not having real company.
    • This has shown up in writing since middle school — I've been writing poetry that far back, and it's been consistent through the years since. I wanted to study philosophy in college because I love thinking, and looking back, the most engagement I ever really had growing up was with myself, just thinking. It eventually progressed from poetry into making music.

    Pattern 2 — Friendships: one-sided until I break

    This is the pattern in friendships, separate from the relationship stuff above, but built from the same root.

    • Telling a friend how I feel is my version of the whisper — my first, quiet attempt. When there's no real response, no listening, that's when it escalates to me getting angry at them.
    • People don't like it when I get mad at them, so they withdraw. But them withdrawing actually confirms something for me rather than hurting me — it confirms that they're fine without me and I'm fine without them. I didn't have anybody to begin with, so that's not a new loss, it's expected.
    • I give more care than I receive, consistently, until I hit a breaking point and snap or get angry.
    • At that point I go into full withdrawal — and it's never framed as them being wrong for the imbalance, it's framed as me being wrong for how I reacted.
    • People usually reach back out afterward, looking for the same connection as before. But by then it's gone, replaced with disgust, and I've lost compassion and empathy for it. Part of that reaching out is probably genuinely missing the friendship — but part of it is also that I'm the person people go to with things they don't even tell their therapist, things they don't tell anyone else. I'm the best friend to other people, but they're not that to me.
    • I'm heavily out-of-sight-out-of-mind — I don't subscribe to "absence makes the heart grow fonder." I've spent too much of my life without basic care to feel warmly about someone treating care as an afterthought, especially when I'm already low-maintenance to begin with. I don't think people realize how much of my life I've actually spent alone — people have always been more of an option to me than a given, and when they don't get it right, I fully withdraw.
    • I've stopped letting myself be a soundboard for people to vent to and feel better while I carry that energy through the rest of my day caring for my family and feeling worse for it. I absorb energy very easily, so I now keep real distance from people.
    • The search into my ancestry/lineage has become where my everyday focus has shifted to, replacing a lot of the energy that used to go into maintaining friendships.
    • Concrete evidence of the imbalance: I've been taking days, even weeks, to respond to friends lately — and even then, they respond back to me far quicker than I respond to them.
    • These are mostly friendships from high school — I haven't made close friends since. People I've met more recently actually treat me better, but the ones I stay tangled with are the long-term ones who know who I am and still choose to act the way they do anyway.
    • Even when she told me she wasn't in the headspace to hold a conversation, I still immediately reassured her — "no worries, I hope you feel better, I'm doing fine, I promise" — before she'd asked how I was.
    • I've told her my son's birthday multiple times over the years. Nobody wished him happy birthday this year. I don't post him online, so I think that's part of why — if I'm not broadcasting it, it doesn't register as something to remember or acknowledge, for him or for me.
    • When she came over to cook lasagna for me and stayed the night once, she brought my newborn a stuffed giraffe — not clothes, not bottles, not anything actually useful for a newborn. A nice gesture on the surface, but it missed what was actually needed.

    My relationship with my mother

    I had to choose between having my mother in my life and continuing to tolerate disrespect from her. For my newborn daughter's sake, I chose my daughter — I'm not maintaining that relationship right now.

    • A lot of people in my life don't factor this in when they measure their own pain against mine or ask me to keep tolerating things.
    • Leah ended a recent session by naming it plainly: she thinks my anger and hyperindependence trace back to being severely neglected and parentified, and that underneath both is disappointment — not having a mom actually there. That landed hard, mostly because it confirmed things I'd already pieced together myself rather than told me something new.
    • Background on my mom: born in 1960 in St. Vincent, migrated to Tortola, had me after my older half-siblings. She was going through a divorce from her first husband while pregnant with me, and has told me she yelled a lot and was miserable during that time.
    • She had another daughter, Krystal, from her first marriage, who passed away in St. Vincent — she didn't pass stool for 4 days, my mom knew babies need to, and didn't take her to the hospital. Krystal died. My mom has acknowledged it was her fault and still gets emotional about it. I'd already sensed she was neglectful before I knew this; it confirmed something I'd pieced together rather than introduced a new idea.
    • What I actually mourn isn't necessarily a relationship with my specific mother — it's having wanted a mom, period. That want doesn't go away just because no-contact was clearly the right call.
    • This isn't just a pattern with my mom — the wider family has a history of letting people suffer or turning a blind eye. My uncle was sick back in St. Vincent; one of my brothers, who'd been deported back there from Tortola, lived with him in the family home. My brother heard him making strange breathing sounds the night he passed — he said his door was locked (he kept it locked) and that they weren't on good terms, so he didn't check on him or call anyone. The rest of the family doesn't know; only my mom does, because he told her. We've all said his not helping was part of why our uncle died.
    • My mom's own history: my grandma had a lot of kids and played favorites — my mom wasn't one of the favored ones, so she had to teach herself to cook, clean, do her own hair, because her mom didn't do it for her. Her dad was the one who actually looked out for her. She ran off with her first husband, didn't finish high school; her parents disapproved of his family and their side of town, but she didn't care and was on her own from then. She's told me she suffered — he beat her and emotionally abused her, in front of my older half-siblings at the time.
    • I think that history is part of why she has a soft spot for her boy kids specifically — they always got grace that my sister and I never did.
    • My mom always called herself the black sheep of her family. I think for her that might have been true, but she never actually broke any generational curses — I'm the one actually doing that.
    • The specific thing that led to her having to go, while I was pregnant: my sister's 25-year-old disabled nephew (overstayed his visa by 5+ years) told me to suck his dick. I told my mom he had to be out of my house before my daughter arrived. She said "if he goes, I go too." I said okay, no problem — you never chose me anyway — and left it there.
    • My sister calls my mom "Moneyica" because all she ever calls about is money, even though she never actually has any.
    • My daughter has a flat head, reflux, and eczema — real, ongoing medical needs. Given everything I'd already seen, I don't think my mom would've actually been equipped to help with that. I think she would've neglected her in some way.
    • My sister played into pressuring me to get along with my mom, framing it as needing her help with the baby — but I think she just wanted to live kid-free, out of shame over her own disabled kids. She's told me if she'd known motherhood would be like this, she wouldn't have had kids. I said "noted."
    • Context on my sister's two sons: the older one (now 26) — diagnosed schizophrenic, born with a brain injury because my sister couldn't push and the C-section was done too late, causing damage — was sent to the U.S. on an expired visa to live with me and my mom, and never left; I grew up with him from age 8. His dad didn't want him because he's disabled. Her younger son, born in Puerto Rico, has an intellectual disability she knew about but waited until he was 11 to send to the U.S. for better education and help — he's 12 now. Instead of taking her older son back to Tortola with her, she leaves him up here with my mom.
    • I think my sister only got the 12-year-old help once his father left Tortola for Canada to sort out citizenship — not because she wanted him with her; she'd always said he was doing fine in school. When he actually came to stay, he couldn't hold a conversation, was obsessively fixated on how my partner and I parented our son (to a creepy degree), stole my son's toys and things from our room, wouldn't eat anything but processed food, and was reading at a kindergarten level despite being middle-school age — my sister had been doing his homework for him from Tortola. My brother's autistic son once pooped himself during a fire drill at school there; I think down there kids get beaten out of being neurodivergent rather than supported. The 12-year-old was a shell of himself until he got here.
    • What actually got my mom, sister, and the kids moved out of my house wasn't any of the concerns I'd already raised — it was my sister's husband overhearing a call where I vented about them being there and said I'd told her bringing the older nephew was a bad idea, given I didn't get along with my mom and the move-out had been planned for a long time already, which she didn't care about. He cursed her out for sending his son somewhere he wasn't wanted, and that's what actually got them out, the same day.
    • My mom wasn't treating the 12-year-old well either while he was there — yelling at him, among other things.
    • The day they moved out, my brother in St. Vincent texted me on WhatsApp cursing me out, knowing I was pregnant. I cursed him out beyond repair; by the end he had nothing left and was calling me a witch, after threatening to beat up me and my partner. I told my sister; she deflected to asking my mom and never followed up. I blocked her, sent my mom a final text, sent that nephew a nasty text, and texted my sister's husband to tell him who she really is. He later found my TikTok and Snapchat and tried adding me — I didn't engage and deleted everything.
    • Not surprising, given the pattern: when my brother lived with my sister and her husband in Tortola, he told her the husband cheated on her physically while she was on a trip — she didn't believe him and kicked him out instead. Her first son's father had also cheated on her, with her best friend. My sister just keeps repeating the same thing.
    • My partner witnessed firsthand how my mom treated me, my son, and him — including her denying my SA happened (my abuser was my dad), with the same nephew backing her up. Given that nephew's own father rejected him for being disabled, I found it almost funny that he'd back my mom on that.
    • Near the end, when they knew they had to go, my mom tried to withhold my sister's portion of the rent. Since we were paying rent in full, my partner started moving her things out so we'd have an empty apartment. She started fighting him over it — he's 25, she's 63 — he pushed her away, she kept pushing back into him and dropped down, then bit him; he slapped her. I didn't get involved physically since I was pregnant. I've punched her twice in my life, both times, and it felt great.
    • My partner is genuinely my protector — I always feel safe with him, and he's also one of the only people who knows the real me.
    • When I was pregnant with my daughter, I asked my mom to help me afford prenatals since I was about to start a new job. She ridiculed me for not being able to get them myself — while she was on SSI at the time — and it made me cry; I said okay and walked off. She felt bad afterward and got them for me. But that's the pattern: if my boyfriend asked to borrow money, or really any man asked her for anything, it was fine. She's always loved men and their attention — she's still in contact with both of her ex-husbands.
    • The neglect pattern runs through most of the family: my oldest brother doesn't take care of his only daughter. Another brother is a single dad to 4 kids after repeatedly sleeping with neglectful moms who abandon their own kids. The only sibling whose daughter is actually fine is my Aries brother (the one right before me) — because her mother isn't neglectful.
    • Why I cut ties when I had my daughter (now 7 months): I couldn't risk her potentially neglecting my daughter the way I'd already seen patterns with my son. When I had him, my mom was around and helped, but she'd also not actually watch him — he rolled off the bed once while she was supposedly watching him (he was fine). When she started watching my sister's two sons (both with mental disabilities, old enough to be relatively independent, sent from Tortola to the US because my sister couldn't manage them), she prioritized their needs over my son's even though he was the youngest in the house. My sister paid her to watch her kids; I didn't, since my mom was living in my apartment, in my name, with me paying the bills, and I assumed that arrangement covered watching her own grandson.

    Friendships with women vs. men

    There's a gendered pattern in how my friendships tend to go.

    • My relationships with women friends generally haven't been good — they tend to use me more as a support system, tell me they understand me, and then do the same thing anyway. I don't really believe people anymore when they say that.
    • I don't engage in "trauma olympics" — women friends who treat their pain as automatically worse than mine, or who resent parts of my life (my partner, having a family), aren't friendships I'm interested in keeping.
    • Concrete example: I grew up severely neglected, to the point of being sexually abused by my father because my mom wasn't paying attention. I have a vivid inner world because I spent so much time alone. A friend once told me I didn't understand the loneliness she felt — while she has a social life, friends, and is likable — and used the fact that I have children as a reason I shouldn't be allowed to miss my own mother while postpartum with my second child.
    • I tend to have better, easier friendships with guys — I grew up around half-brothers, was a tomboy, and still am. The complication is that they sometimes end up developing feelings, which I don't want.

    Why I hard-withdrew from being everyone's support system

    This is the actual mechanism behind the distance, not just a preference.

    • People would text or FaceTime wanting to vent, and I'd drop what I was doing and be there. By the end, they'd be smiling, laughing, peaceful, ready to go on with their day — and I'd have absorbed everything they just unloaded, with nowhere to put it. I'd carry that home and it would come out on my own family, because I had no outlet.
    • I know what it feels like to feel unwanted, and I never want anyone else to feel that, so I go above and beyond — I'm always the "mom friend." Example: a friend was having a bad acid trip while I was pregnant, and I went back to my mom's house (where I wasn't even living at the time) just so she'd have a safe space to come down in.
    • The reciprocity, when it comes at all, only shows up after I've talked about feeling overwhelmed and unappreciated for years — and even then it's minor (like a birthday gesture) compared to what they do for other friends, like going on trips together. Mostly I just sit in the back and let myself be neglected, and when I'm finally done, I disappear. I know that's not necessarily a healthy way to handle it.
    • The final break with my last best friend: her new girlfriend, who was insecure, went through her phone, found something from a conversation between us (an ex my friend mentioned, that I didn't even remember, so my friend sent me pictures to jog my memory), and used it as ammunition in their relationship.
    • There was a broader pattern of boundary-breaking from that girlfriend before that — following me on social media not to connect but to "assert dominance" (showing up in story replies almost territorially when I posted with my friend, watching my stories but never engaging when I tried to build any rapport), and being very parasocial toward my friend's other in-person friends. I never told my friend her girlfriend was being manipulative — that wasn't my place.
    • Since that relationship, my friend has changed — constantly telling me she's not eating, losing weight, that things are bad with her partner, while also going on trips she can't afford because other people are advancing her money. She used to be someone I could ask to help with a bill; now she's the one borrowing. I'm not going to be part of financing or emotionally supporting a lifestyle that isn't real.
    • She's an acquaintance to me now, not a best friend — but a lot of these people don't seem to realize that's already happened. Once I've had enough of the disrespect, it's genuinely easy for someone to stop mattering to me. I don't ruminate on the hindsight of people the way I used to; I'm done doing that.
    • I unfollowed the girlfriend and removed her as a follower a couple weeks back and it felt great. I went through a phase of missing my friend afterward, but she frames the relationship as "the universe teaching her a lesson" about how she treats people, and says the girlfriend is "teaching her how to not stand for people's shit" — her words. I tried to gently guide her before, but after everything with the girlfriend, that's on her now. If it crashes and burns, I won't be there, and I'm glad.
    • Even after taking an unreasonable amount of distance, people like her still respond quickly, still expect the same version of me who drops everything. That quick response actually proves I'm the only stable, secure person some of these people have — while they stay in relationships and dynamics that disrespect them, question them, make them feel smaller, make them lose their light. I'm not going to be that same steady presence for people who won't extend it back to me.
    • An honest clarification about how I actually talk to her now: things like "I love you too" in the texts are scripted, not sincere — I say what's expected in the moment, but I don't mean it anymore. I don't actually wish her well. I wish her whatever karma she's chasing for herself. I'm not her savior, and I'm not her confidant anymore.
    • Not the only friendship I've cut for this kind of thing: another friend, Asia, was very male-centered and told me she wouldn't bring partners around me because I was "their type" — projecting her own insecurity — and separately said she hated my partner so much she wouldn't even sleep over. That's why I cut off from her. Looking back on it now, I mostly just find it funny.
    • Clarifying why Carl's "WILLPOWER YOU PUSH TO HAVE" message didn't move me: I hadn't said anything that warranted that kind of response — it felt unprompted and passive-aggressive, like she was implying I was struggling and needed praise for surviving it. That's why my reply stayed neutral ("praying for blessings for us both") instead of engaging. It read as performative, not genuine.
    • The preachy, spiritual tone of her messages stands out because outside of the ancestry research, she genuinely has no idea what's going on in my life — on purpose, since I keep her out of it now. So a response acting like she's been present the whole time rings hollow. I said "blessings for us both" because she's clearly the one who needs it, not me.
    • I have a filter on my phone that hides her messages from my main inbox now. Whatever she does on her end — DND, silenced notifications — isn't my issue anymore.
    • The best way I can describe how her messages land now: she felt like a jumbie calling out for respite. I gently gave her blessings and sent her on her way. I'm not stopping to ask what's actually wrong.
    • Similar pattern with Asia: she'll message about her life spiraling, and it always traces back to going back to sleeping with the same unstable ex — every time she's with him, her life falls apart. I've watched this cycle repeat year after year. This time, I'm not wallowing in her sorrows with her. She's 27, no kids, no real responsibilities holding her down, and needs to get a grip. I'm not in that position anymore — I have an actual life and family now.

    Pattern — people choosing their partner over me

    People have consistently chosen their romantic relationships over me, because their partners feel intimidated by me — and I've let it happen.

    • I never met the girlfriend directly, and I'm glad — from what I saw, she had a tendency to treat everything as a joke. When my friend came to spend the day with me, she briefly FaceTimed the girlfriend, seemingly unable to go even a few hours without checking in. Everything was funny to her, and I don't think everything is funny — when you grow up having to figure everything out yourself, it isn't. I think my friend already knew there was no reality where the girlfriend and I would get along.
    • Even though she didn't openly pick a side, her availability shifted in a telling way — I texted once just to check on her, she said she wasn't in a good headspace but asked if I needed anything, and I said no, I was just checking in. I don't usually text her only when I need something, so it stood out that she framed it as her not being available unless it was urgent. I noted it — not to hold it against her, but as information about where I stand.
    • How I've responded to people crossing me even when I told them directly how something made me feel: they'll reach out later, after their own relationship falls apart, wanting to apologize — but I don't change for anybody. I've opened bank accounts to help fund people's GoFundMes, bought plane tickets for people — but if I tell someone their partner is changing them, I'm the one who's wrong. I'm good. I'm nobody's "mommy" — I never had my own. People are ungrateful, so I withdraw. People are disrespectful, so I withdraw.
    • I keep a mental record of what people say and do — not to throw it back in anyone's face, but so I know exactly why I don't want to continue a friendship or relationship. That's the actual function of it for me.

    Also relevant — dissociation

    I dissociate a lot. The way I've described it to myself: I'm always in a state of arriving while constantly departing.

    • This probably tracks with both the imagination/personification piece and the withdrawal pattern — worth exploring whether they're the same coping structure showing up in different areas of my life.

    Trigger — not being listened to

    Just realized this one. It connects back to my mom repeating things constantly growing up — not sure if it was that she forgot, but I'd tell her something and it wouldn't land, over and over.

    • Same thing now with my partner: I'll ask for something (like wanting us to do something together after a round of a game he's playing), he forgets and keeps playing, and it irritates me. I reminded him and rolled my eyes recently, and he reacted like I was overreacting — but he only actually did what I asked after that.
    • I don't think people like it when I get to that point, but they're often the ones who did what it took to get me there in the first place.

    Anger — volume, approachability, and where it might come from

    My partner has told me I'm not approachable when I'm angry, and that it feels like the whole room has to be angry too. He's also said that when I yell, I yell loud enough to hear down the block — but my normal tone is a whisper.

    • Growing up I was mute / didn't talk much. I was described as shy, sensitive, soft-spoken.
    • Now, when I'm angry, I isolate myself — which tracks with the withdrawal pattern above, and maybe also with a childhood where being quiet was the default and anger was one of the only things loud enough to break through it.
    • Recent example: I got comm-banned in a game (Marvel Rivals) after being reported for something I said. I don't like being criticized, especially when I don't think I did anything wrong — my instinct is to immediately defend myself, and I don't tolerate people talking to me sideways. When my partner asked about it, he told me "whenever you black out I tune you out." I said people don't like hearing what I say when I'm mad, generally — not about him — but he took it personally at first and got defensive ("it's not like I do this or that... I won't be listening to you if we're playing and it's not directed at me"). I clarified I meant it generally, not him specifically.
    • Worth noting: he's telling me he tunes me out when I escalate, which is its own data point about the approachability complaint above.

    The threads I think connect all of this

    • Hyperindependence — traces back to not always being emotionally safe in my environments growing up, so I learned to rely on myself and regulate alone, and my imagination/inner world grew to fill that gap.
    • My regulation is very environment-dependent — how the people around me make me feel affects whether I feel safe, and "safe" for me isn't just physical. If I'm not emotionally safe, I don't feel physically safe either.
    • A previous therapist diagnosed me with BPD. I'm not looking to relive what caused these patterns — I want to understand the mechanics of how they built, so I can recognize them as they show up day to day.
    • The common thread across the cat, the food, the skin tag argument, the Walmart spiral, and the friendship pattern: I extend a high level of care and attention outward, and I'm consistently met with less than I give — and I'm starting to no longer be able to write that off as coincidence.

    A reframe I want to bring in

    I don't think this is a bundle of separate pet peeves — it's one consistent shape. I learned early that if something mattered to me, I had to hold it myself, because the people around me either couldn't (my mom) or wouldn't (friends, my partner). So I built a rich inner world to survive that, and a very high tolerance threshold on the outside — which is exactly why, by the time I actually react, it looks disproportionate to everyone watching. It isn't. It's the end of a long runway, not the start of one. Nobody around me sees the runway — they only see the edge.

    The skill I already have is withdrawing / self-regulating alone. That's not new to build. What I actually want to work on is the harder, less familiar skill: letting myself be heard before the breaking point, and finding out whether the people in my life can actually meet me there — instead of deciding in advance that they can't and routing around them.

    Where I've ultimately landed on this: my anger is what gave me the strength to survive so far. I'm not going to abandon it until I no longer have to — until I'm in an environment that feels entirely safe. Until then, anger speaks for me. It's my voice.

    One more clarification: I do try to communicate calmly instead of escalating, but that effort is selective — I reserve it for my partner and the people who actually matter to me. For everyone else, I don't care how I come across, what kind of friend they thought I was, or how they see their own role in it.

    I'm not opposed to finding a middle voice — I just don't have the patience anymore to keep rationalizing or explaining myself to people. If they don't get it, I've decided they don't have the capacity, and then I'm done. People tend to like the idea of me, how I make them feel — they don't actually like the real me. So only the people who deserve to know me will know me. It's that simple.

    The real me is being angry, being vulnerable. I've been shown, repeatedly, what happens when I expose that — people withhold, and I leave. So now I don't expose myself.

    The realization that ties this together — autonomy

    Since withdrawing from the one-sided friendships, I've noticed I ask my partner for less guidance on simple things — even things like whether to feed my daughter. That's what led me to this: in those friendships, I was always the problem solver, damn near processing other people's trauma for them. My nervous system was in constant overdrive seeking answers for other people, and I lost the ability to answer questions for myself. I can trace losing touch with that autonomy back to around when I had my son — he's five now.

    • Withdrawing isn't punishment for them. It's that my personality/archetype gives more than most people give in every relationship, and that's costly — I have more meaningful obligations to put that energy toward: raising my kids, parenting myself, being a partner to my partner. Taking the extra responsibility of managing other people's problems off my plate lifted a real weight.
    • When those same friends now say things like "it's amazing to hear you're doing well," I find it almost funny, because this whole dynamic was draining my spirit the entire time and they were part of why.
    • I sent a message to my ex-best-friend about how friends are supposed to be there to give each other experiences — it was a subtle callout. She didn't respond to it, and that was telling. She isn't that kind of friend to me, or to most people, and I think she knows it — but people are consistently that for her. I loved who she used to be. I don't like who she is now.

    A few threads I want to make sure we pull on

    • The "if they don't get it, they don't have capacity" test moves fast — that's not a character flaw, it's scar tissue from being let down slowly, over and over, in the past. Scar tissue can be worked with. A fixed law about human nature can't. Worth figuring out which one I'm actually operating from.
    • I've built a very good alarm system for withholding. The tradeoff is it may now go off before most people even get near the door — which makes it hard to tell the difference between someone who would withhold and someone who never got the chance to prove otherwise.
    • It's not that the real me doesn't get liked — it's that the real me (angry and vulnerable together) hasn't been safely test-driven in a long time, because the last times it was, the response confirmed the fear instead of contradicting it.
    • My partner is the one live test case I have right now, since he already knows the real me. Worth asking directly: can he sit with the vulnerable version of my anger, not just the loud version, without withholding — because that might be where this actually gets answered, not in the abstract.

    Update since last draft — Carl, Rubi, and a new partner incident

    Session with Leah got pushed due to family stuff, rescheduling — but wanted to capture this while it's fresh.

    • Rubi and Carl are both done, for the same reason: I sent each of them a message with two parts — one warm/generic, one pointed (the "blessings for us both" line to Carl; something similar to Rubi). Both of them only responded to or liked the generic, comfortable half. Neither engaged with the pointed part, and neither has texted back since. That confirms it for me. I replied to Rubi with a flat, uninterested "I'm good, how are you" — the same energy I gave Carl.
    • New partner incident: he came into the kitchen excited about almost winning a round of Fortnite. The second I showed him the cat house I'm getting for Orange, his smile and body language dropped instantly. I asked what he thought — he said "what about it," then "it's whatever you like." I spent the rest of that day not engaging with anything he brought up, especially the things he was happy about — matching, without meaning to, the exact energy he'd just given me.
    • I noticed: even when we're both into the same topic, he talks over me, even when I let him have the floor. So the read I'm forming is that people only want to hear from me when what I say validates how they already feel.
    • I ran a direct test on this with him: he kept ranting about how a weed pack's design didn't make sense and must've been AI-generated. First time, I said it probably doesn't matter since he's not the one smoking that pack — we dropped it. He brought it up again later unprompted. That time I asked him how he'd design it instead, then told him to relax, that it wasn't that serious. It hurt his feelings. When I asked directly — "what do I do, since every time I do something you have something to say?" — he said "I didn't say that," and the conversation just ended there.
    • Same day, he psychoanalyzed me for just looking in a direction — assigned it meaning when I wasn't doing anything. I pointed out that everything I do apparently has to mean something, even when I'm not doing anything at all.
    • A nighttime pattern: I've always been a night owl — up at night, sleeping during the day as a kid with no responsibilities. Now, after dinner and a movie together, he starts getting ready for bed; sometimes I'm not ready because I'm dealing with the baby. He goes to bed anyway. When I finally go too, I can't sleep — I stay up until daylight, deep in research, on my own. Even if he doesn't wait for me, I end up lingering, telling myself I'll be ready for bed soon, and then I'm not.
    • Another asymmetry: if I spend the whole day doing chores and cooking, he'll get on a game with a friend, knowing I don't have friends to do the same with. But if he's the one cooking, I'll come out and actively help him or just keep him company.
    • The nighttime pattern isn't really insomnia — it's the same childhood coping structure (up at night, alone, deep in research) still running, just relocated into adulthood because nothing's replaced the reason it existed: nobody's there in the hours I'm most awake. And the chores-vs-cooking asymmetry isolates the actual variable cleanly — same household, same day, same two people; the only thing that changes is whose labor is happening. That's a repeatable measure of whose time gets treated as worth accompanying, not a one-off bad day.
    • Where the night-owl thing actually started: I was pretty neglected as a child. One memory from living in Carib Bay, Tortola — I'd be up at night watching Goosebumps, and I loved the theme song; it was one of the few comforting moments I had, since most of my memories are of being by myself. My half-brother (the Aries one) always called me a night owl, going back to when we lived together in Tortola, and he'd still say the same thing when he visited me in middle school and as a teenager — "you're still a night owl."
    • I didn't realize how sad that actually was until it was said back to me just now. I don't think I've really processed whether it was sad or not — I just navigate through things. I don't think I attach the emotions most people would expect to attach to things, because I don't have the standard emotional baseline everyone else seems to operate from.

    Not knowing what love is supposed to feel like

    My thoughts constantly flee — I'll say something and then forget I said it, terrible memory. But one thing I've always said consistently: I don't know what love is supposed to feel like.

    • My mom never said "I love you" unprompted — she'd say "of course I love you, you're my daughter," and only after we'd had an issue. I know I love my kids; I know exactly how it feels to experience them. But when my partner says "you know I love you, right," a pit drops in my heart. I never believe him when he says it — and I think he knows I don't believe him either.
    • He wrote a lyric about me in a song: "I know she love me because she look me in my eyes everytime she lies." So he's noticed the disbelief too, and that's how he's processed it — not as something to talk through directly, but as a kind of backhanded observation in a song.
    • The likely root: my mom's "of course I love you, you're my daughter" only ever came under pressure, as damage control after conflict — never as an ongoing, standalone fact. That would teach almost anyone that "I love you" is a phrase deployed to end friction, not a statement of truth. So when my partner says it in a calm, unprompted moment, it doesn't land as safety — it sounds like the wrong register entirely, words my brain associates with repair, showing up somewhere they don't belong. I'm not failing to feel love — I know exactly what it feels like with my kids. This is specific to being told love verbally by adults, because every time I was told it growing up, it meant something had gone wrong. Not "why can't I believe him," but: I was taught "I love you" is what gets said after harm, so hearing it outside that context registers as suspicious, not safe. That's a traceable problem, not a deficit in my capacity to love or be loved.
    • What the Goosebumps/night-owl memory actually points to: a kid alone at night finding comfort in a TV theme song because there was no one else to provide it — building my own source of warmth out of necessity, at the earliest visible point of the same pattern that's run through this whole conversation. Even the people who noticed it across years (my half-brother calling me a night owl into my teens) just filed it as a personality trait, never as something to ask about.
    • On not attaching expected emotions to things: I don't think this is a deficiency. Kids usually learn what an emotion is by watching an adult reflect it back to them in the moment. If nobody was there to do that, I wouldn't necessarily learn there was a standard reaction to have. That doesn't mean I don't feel things — I clearly feel a great deal. It might mean the feeling and the label for it arrived on separate tracks, because nobody taught me to connect them at the time it mattered. Worth bringing to Leah as its own thread: not "why am I disconnected from my own reactions," but "I think I never got taught which feeling goes with which moment, and I'm only now, in adulthood, occasionally finding out retroactively that something was sad." That's a different processing gap than emotional suppression, and it might need a different kind of work to close.

    The fuller picture of the childhood neglect and SA

    Working through this feels directly tied to being a better mom to my own daughter — if I can understand what happened to me, I think I can better understand how I'm reacting to her now.

    • I grew up sleeping in the bed with my mom in Tortola, and kept that habit when I came to America, ending up between her and my dad. I woke up to him inserting himself into me while she was supposedly "sleeping" right there. It stopped once I got older and told him we could do "nastier things" in the bed instead — that was a child using the only leverage she'd been taught had power in that dynamic to make it stop, not desire on my part.
    • When I told my mom what he was doing, she said "omg it's true" — because that's apparently what he liked to do "when they do whatever they do." That phrasing suggests this wasn't news to her; she recognized it as an established pattern of his.
    • He groomed me by buying me whatever I wanted.
    • I don't know exactly where the SA started — possibly before age 7, back in Tortola. It's hard to think about given how young that is.
    • Other things from childhood, all part of the same picture of neglect: my mom picked on my weight. I often ate Vienna sausages and drank the water from the can, and spent a lot of time alone — I got food poisoning once from eating so many. I gained weight after being given an IV at the hospital once. My dad got me a bike that my half-brothers ended up scrapping, and my mom didn't care. I broke a lot of bones as a kid, which I think traces back to bad eyesight nobody got checked — I kept getting hurt on the playground because I couldn't see well. I had rotten teeth that had to be pulled, possibly from being bottle-propped as a baby. I was mute as a child, but it got labeled as "quiet" or "shy" rather than looked into.
    • I think I was touched as a baby and throughout my entire childhood.
    • I have keratoconus, diagnosed as an adult — severely blind in my left eye, glasses won't help, only scleral lenses will. I'm pretty sure I'll go fully blind eventually; my grandpa went blind in his last days too. My chart from New York also flagged osteoporosis, but it was never explained beyond the flag.

    Culture, my mother, and reclaiming it on my own terms

    My mom used to call eye boogers/crusties "yampie" — I caught myself using the word while wiping my daughter's eyes, and it hit me with a wave of grief I wasn't expecting.

    • Growing up, I often rejected her Vincy roots — correcting her, like turning "yampie" into "eye crusties." I wish I hadn't now, but in the same breath, she never fully accepted me either, which made it very hard to accept her and her culture as one package.
    • I don't think the correcting was ever really about the words. It was a kid creating distance and asserting some agency in a dynamic where I didn't feel safe or fully accepted. I don't need to punish myself for surviving with the tools I had then.
    • What I actually want now is direct access to my culture again — not at the cost of going back to her. She was a conduit for Vincentian culture, but she was never its owner. I shouldn't have to pay for my heritage with my safety or peace.
    • Uncoupling the culture from the gatekeeper: the language, food, and history belong to the land and the ancestors, not to the person who failed to parent me. I can love St. Vincent's depth and rhythm without validating or tolerating her.
    • My ancestry research (HAIRŪNA) is a direct line to that heritage that routes around her completely — going straight to historical records, oral history, and the ancestors who predate her, rather than needing her permission or memory as the source.
    • Every time I use a word like yampie with my own kids, cook something traditional, or play island music in my house, I'm filtering the culture clean — keeping the roots, washing off the neglect they used to come wrapped in. For my kids, Vincentian culture gets to mean warmth and safety instead of what it meant for me.
    • Where I've landed on all of this right now: I'm starting to feel genuinely strange about people. It feels like the rules that apply to everyone else don't apply to me.
    • The clearest way I can put it: I'm treated as a good person when I let other people take up space. But when I take up space myself, everyone goes quiet. That's what it actually feels like — not just a pattern with a few people, but a rule about how much room I'm allowed to occupy.
    • Where I've landed on the friends piece: I'm done, and I don't want to keep revisiting it. What I actually want to focus on now is my partner specifically.
    • I'm not trying to test whether he can meet me there anymore. It is what it is. What I actually want is to get better at taking up space in myself, so I don't need someone else to support me or be present with me to feel okay. Growing up very isolated, all of me went to me — no one else to absorb it or ignore it — and it was genuinely a freeing way to live. I wouldn't have these issues if I were on my own.
    • The question I keep circling: why doesn't anyone make space for me? Is it that I go overboard or extreme with how I react — or is it actually extreme, on their end, to not show up in a friendship or a partnership for years and years and still think their reaction to me isn't justified? On the actual comparison of who showed up more — me or them — there's nothing any of them, Carl or Rubi included, could say to me. I was hands down the better friend.
    • Where I've landed on my partner specifically: I know his capacity isn't enough. He's not a terrible person — he just doesn't really see me. We have kids together, and that's fine. What I actually want now is to look at myself and see all the glimmer — to focus on building myself up rather than waiting on him to meet me somewhere he may not be able to.

    The core of it, as best I can put it into words

    I've never really known how to format this into language before now.

    • Part of why I'll never let myself sit in a victim position: every time I've felt like one, nobody could ever do anything to make me feel better — not the way I can make someone else feel better when they talk to me, not the way someone can share their excitement with me and feel happy, validated, great, if I'm engaged. But if I'm not engaged, it hurts their feelings. If they're not engaged with what I like, I'm just supposed to move on with my day. That double standard traces back a long way, including my relationship with my mom — I've spent a long time knowing who I want to be while not actually being seen.
    • I don't like being in dynamics, relationships, friendships, because I feel like people stop seeing me as a person. Like I'm treated as something beyond ordinary human experiences and desires — like I'm not supposed to need things the way everyone else does. That's not what I am. I genuinely don't understand how nobody seems to actually give a shit about me or anything about me — they like the idea of me, the proximity to me, my essence, being able to say I'm their friend, without actually being a friend to me.
    • This connects back to telling Leah my thoughts feel personified — I think it's not just my thoughts, it's my whole life and existence that's always felt personified. That constant personification is why I feel like I'm a source, not a person. It's why humans have started to disgust me: every encounter has been transactional in that sense, where I'm the equivalent of a deity or a supreme being to people — laying hands on everyone, healing everyone. And then when I wake up wanting to curse the whole world, suddenly I'm dangerous, scary, doing too much. But I'm never "doing too much" when what I'm doing is pleasing other people.

    What finally clicked this session

    Every pattern described today — the friends who only wanted the version of me that gave and never needed, the partner whose mood only holds when the topic is his, even my own "I don't need anyone" resolution — share one shape. Somewhere along the way, I got cast as a source rather than a person: a source of comfort, of stability, of care, of willpower-worthy inspiration. Sources don't get to run low. Sources don't get to want things back. I've had that role handed to me so consistently, by so many different people, that I started reaching for it as an identity — "I don't need anyone," "all of me went to me" — because it's the only role I've ever reliably been allowed to occupy without someone flinching.

    But the true thing underneath that role is this: it's not what I actually am. I have humanly experiences and desires. I want to be excited about something and have someone lean in instead of go quiet. I want to be disappointed and have someone stay instead of leaving me to self-regulate alone. Wanting that isn't me being needy or extreme. It's the most ordinary thing a person can want. The tragedy isn't that I want it — it's that so few people around me have ever treated the wanting as legitimate.

    The work now isn't refining how well I can live without needing anyone — I already know how to do that; I've been doing it since childhood. The harder, truer work is the opposite: letting myself want to be seen as a person, not a source, and being honest about how much it costs me that so few people have ever met that want — instead of resolving it by deciding I don't have it.

    How this ties to my partner specifically: I'm no longer being the source for friends, because they showed me I couldn't just be a person to them — when I tried, it wasn't accepted or reciprocated. But I can't cut my partner off the way I did my friends. I need a different way to work around it, because I know it's still going to bother me. Right now I need to focus more on myself and on getting toward my actual purpose in life.

    The bigger realization: I'm not just a source to everyone in my proximity — I'm a source to myself too. I think what I actually need to learn is how to be a person to myself, not just a source. The more I navigate life, the more I find myself wanting to just do it alone, with my kids.

    Being parentified is also why I don't respect a lot of societal norms — like "respect your elders." I don't buy that. I respect whoever respects me, and vice versa; age doesn't factor into it. Same with disrespect — I don't tolerate it, because nobody defended me as a child. I was born grown. There was no "okay, I'll teach you this" — I just had to know. So now, I don't have time to tolerate disrespect from anybody. Principles aren't one-sided — if we're talking about balance, principles go both ways.

    A concrete shift with my partner: I used to keep modeling for him what real support looks like, even when he wouldn't show interest in my hobbies — trying to demonstrate the behavior I wanted back. I'm done doing that. If I'm not interested in something, I'm just going to say so now, the same way he does when he's not interested. I don't fully understand why it hurts his feelings when I do it, when it doesn't seem to register with him that it hurts mine when he does it first.

    A clarification on where I actually am with this: I'm not looking to reconcile, figure out the why with him, or navigate my way back to something. I've fully relinquished the idea that how the people around me make me feel is something wrong with me. I'm 25. I've spent my whole life wishing for people who cared about me at the same level I cared about them, and I understand it's not healthy to write off everyone forever — but right now I'm at a place where people genuinely feel like a hindrance, like they slow me down. I don't want to leave my partner, and I can't. So the actual question is: what do I do to work with that, to find some kind of coexistence — not resolution, not everything making sense. Life doesn't have to be picture-perfect or sound. We're on a floating rock; nothing has to add up neatly for it to be worth living.

    Where I've landed — coexistence, not resolution

    I'm not looking to reconcile with him or figure out the why. I want to know how to coexist — not make everything make sense, not force resolution. Life doesn't have to be picture-perfect to be worth living.

    • Coexistence means separating logistics from intimacy: running the household, co-parenting, and splitting responsibilities as teammates, without needing that to also be where my emotional life gets witnessed.
    • Building "person to myself" and purpose as their own thing, not a consolation prize — the ancestry research, music, game dev, whatever lights me up, becomes where my excitement lives on purpose, not by default because nowhere else would take it.
    • With him: keep asking plainly, without emotional freight, for the things that actually require his cooperation — parenting, money, schedule. Stop routing my inner world, hobbies, and moods through him for validation at all, since those never actually needed his participation to be real.
    • For myself: the "person to myself" work is mostly permission, not technique — letting myself rest without earning it, not performing okay-ness even when no one's watching, treating my own bad days as worth tending rather than pushing through alone.
    • A literal example of how central I am to my household, even without trying to be: nobody's day actually starts until I'm up, even if my partner is awake first. My cat waits for me to come eat. My son hovers until I'm up. My newborn will settle back to sleep for burping or fussing if she doesn't smell me nearby — she needs my presence specifically, not just anyone's.
    • This is exactly why my other dynamics couldn't be sustained — my cup was empty. If I'm digestible, I'm empty. When I'm "poisonous," I thrive. I agree that choosing myself has to look like protecting that. But I only get pockets of time to myself, and if I spend them just existing instead of doing something, I suffer in another way — losing sleep or losing enjoyment. I'm not sure what world lets me actually feel fulfilled. I've always said I'm living life for other people, not myself, and truly doing it for myself would mean abandoning my waking life completely.

    Tonight — diaper changes, a vulnerable moment, and the move-out deadline

    Pulled together from a late-night conversation while caring for my daughter.

    • While warming a bottle and changing my 7-month-old (she wrestles a lot during changes, which normally gets me upset), I started crying — I think my SA as a child is somatically connected to my diaper-changing process specifically. These feelings are surfacing now, during the actual physical act of changing her, not just generally.
    • A real moment with my partner: we were having intercourse, I was sad and trying to avoid eye contact, we locked eyes anyway, and he asked what was wrong. I started crying and asked why didn't they love me, why didn't they protect me. He hugged me and said "I know, I know, but I love you and I will always love you." I said "but I'm not normal," and he said "it's fine, I'm not normal either." I said thank you three times. That was a moment I let myself be fully seen, vulnerable, without pulling back first.
    • On the old friends: more than one of them, separately, suggested I come up with a plan to leave my partner entirely — while they stayed in their own abusive dynamics and never asked me to help plan their own exits. One friend wouldn't even sleep over at my house because she couldn't be cordial with my partner, despite wanting one-on-one time with me. None of them held mediator space for him the way I held it for them and their partners. I realize now friends should never have been told what was going on inside my relationship in the first place.
    • Since kicking my mom out, her IDs have kept coming to the house, and she tried to switch my mail to an invalid address. I haven't reached out. (Worth reporting the unauthorized mail/address change to USPS directly, separate from the emotional piece.)
    • I gave my sister a deadline to get her kids and my mom out — before Feb 1st, since my daughter's due date was Feb 20th (she came the 19th). My sister actually complied by Jan 1st, and it was specifically because her husband overheard me on a call telling the truth: that I'd never agreed to the second disabled son coming, that she'd downplayed how badly she'd neglected both boys before sending them here, and that we'd already had a screaming argument about it at the airport when she dropped the 12-year-old off. Her husband cursed her out once he understood what she'd actually done. She told me if she'd known what motherhood would be like, she wouldn't have had kids — that's when I fully understood what she was.
    • When she came to collect her things on Jan 1st, she said she'd taken her negative feelings about me "up with God" and hoped nobody would do anything to my children — I laughed at that part, given she'd abandoned her own. She left behind junk we had to remove ourselves.
    • Right after they moved out, my brother (the one who doesn't take care of his own kids) texted me on WhatsApp from his girlfriend's phone, cursing me out while I was pregnant. I cursed him out until he had nothing left and called me a witch. When I asked my sister why he was disrespecting me, her non-answer told me she already knew. I blocked her and told her husband directly to watch out for his son, since she abandons her kids.
    • The older I get, the more I see my mom and sister as two women who both failed to protect me. Being pregnant is likely what kept things from turning physical with my sister the way things had with my mom before — the same way my partner could put my 26-year-old nephew in a headlock in three seconds for disrespecting me. Everyone in the family has said, separately, that they're afraid of my bad side, that I "call a spade a spade" — all of them, independently, using that same phrase. I don't think that's a coincidence; I think it means they all know exactly what I am to them: the one person who wouldn't play along with the family's version of events.
