    Why leaving work to care for my daughter makes sense, and the bow-leg/broken-bones history

    On the brother text: I was the one who told him to "boss up or kill himself" — he's much older than me, 25, and talking to me the way he was, after doing less with his life than I have. Context for that exchange.

    • On leaving my job: I don't think my partner was actually neglecting her — his parenting was probably just normal. But my body reacted to it as neglect, especially because she has real, ongoing needs: reflux, a flat head, eczema, and I'm pretty sure a milk allergy. She's often uncomfortable — overheating, needing to burp 5-6 times before she'll settle — even while smiling and seeming happy. I realized she was uncomfortable underneath the happy surface, and that while I was at work I was barely interacting with her, and when I did, I didn't have the energy to. I couldn't keep working after realizing that.
    • On the bow legs: I've been researching traditional, highly skilled bone-setting doctors as part of my ancestry work, and I think my dad declining that correction did more harm than good, though I haven't fully traced the connection yet.
    • My broken-bone history as a kid, now that I know about the undiagnosed eyesight (keratoconus): I broke my left arm twice as a baby/toddler, including once while my mom was putting my shoes on — not sure if that one traces to her not paying attention. I broke bones twice on the monkey bars — once in primary school when I lingered alone after everyone had gone inside at recess, once again later when it was raining. In middle school, I was nervous about roller skating for the first time, partly because of my known history of breaking bones — something nobody had ever actually looked into. Someone held my hand for about two seconds, then let go. I fell and fractured my right tibia (or fibula) along with the growth plate. My right leg has been a little off ever since.

    A few more childhood memories

    • When people ask me "three things about yourself," my go-to answers tend to be traumatizing facts rather than normal ones — things like "I've broken a lot of bones," "I like poetry," "I was born in Tortola." That's just become my default way of introducing myself.
    • A memory I keep returning to: being in elementary school in the Bronx when my mom left the country — I think for my grandpa's passing in St. Vincent, though I'm not fully sure that's why. She didn't take me.
    • I was in school and after-school/acting programs as a kid. I remember being in class, close to when after-school would end and I'd be with my dad, and starting to cry — not sure anymore if something happened or if I was just acting it, since acting was already a thing for me by then.
    • English teachers always loved me — I had a vivid imagination and tended to run on with details in my writing. Run-on sentences were basically my signature critique.
    • The fallout from that fracture: I missed my middle school prom and graduation entirely, since the school had steps with no way to navigate them in a full leg cast. The classmate who'd let go of my hand felt bad about it — she and I were just classmates, not close — and came over with a teddy bear and spent a little time with me, though I'm pretty sure her mom made her do it. She said she'd visit again. She didn't, really. A lot of people in my life were just genuinely terrible to me.

    The first disclosure, the skateboard moment, and seeking agency as a teen

    • The first time I ever told anyone about my SA, it was my first boyfriend, in high school. Not only did he make me feel "disgusting" when I told him, he made intimacy itself feel weird for me afterward. That reaction made me feel so disgusting I wanted to kill myself. That was the first and formative test of what happens when I let someone in on the truth.
    • My partner wants to teach our son to skateboard the way he knows how. I told my partner I'm afraid to try because I break things so easily, and he said "you just have to learn how to fall." Watching him teach our son ordinary things like that — how to fall, how to ride a bike — makes me realize how much I didn't have on a basic level growing up.
    • As a teenager, I went through a phase of hypersexuality — not about wanting relationships, but specifically around losing my virginity on my own terms. I met someone a couple years older than me online, who lived in Queens while I was in the Bronx. I had my dad drive me there, and found my own way back home by train afterward. Looking back, I understand now that I was trying to make sure my first time happened on my terms, with someone I'd chosen, because I knew if I didn't take control of it, it would end up happening within the abusive dynamic with my dad instead. I didn't have the language for that at the time, but that's what I was actually doing.
    • I also traveled alone a lot as a kid/teen without much caution — far into Queens and the Long Island area with a friend, to Philadelphia by myself just to get my hair done. My mom was never home and never paid attention to where I was, so I just did what I wanted.

    The fuller history — how the abuse was structured, and my mom's role

    Writing this down so I don't have to keep holding it alone in my head. I've processed this by myself for years; this is the first time someone has actually sat with me through it.

    • The first disclosure in high school was to my first boyfriend, not a friend — and his "disgusting" reaction is what made intimacy feel wrong for me afterward.
    • How I got the abuse to change/reduce as a child: I negotiated with my dad that we'd be able to do more as I got older (into high school), and in the meantime it was anal penetration — he'd do it and stop. This happened with my mom on the bed, pretending to be asleep; he'd kiss me a little in front of her, then step out of the room briefly, and it would happen. I believe she knew.
    • When my mom came to the U.S., she was hyper-fixated on getting everyone's immigration papers sorted, even though the older kids were already adults. She didn't buy me clothes — I wore her hand-me-downs, which is also why my sister asked if I liked girls. The only things I was given were electronics, because that's what my dad groomed me with — so I learned to ask for things, not needs, since needs were never going to be met anyway.
    • I have sensory memory (taste, skin) of engaging in sexual acts with other kids, mostly girls from what I remember, that I know happened even though I can't always reconstruct the full context — trauma memory doesn't always arrive as a complete story.
    • My mom's own account of being pregnant with me wasn't good — she was going through a divorce from her abusive first husband at the time, and my dad was the one helping her. The more I learn about my history, the more I think she was with my dad partly because his family had money (his relative owns Big Ben's, a convenience store in Tortola). I have a fragment of memory from a trip to Barbados to finalize visas — being at a bar with my dad, pieces that come back without full context.
    • Putting it plainly: I think my mom sold me, in effect — prioritizing her own paperwork and stability over protecting me, while the abuse was actively happening in her own home.

    I've already confronted my mom with this — her response is its own confirmation

    These aren't new realizations for me — I've said all of this to my mom directly before, including that I felt like she sold me and that she's never prioritized my safety. Every time, she had nothing real to say. That's part of how I know it's true: not denial, not sadness, just deflection into insulting me or saying I don't care about my own kid.

    • How the family actually found out: my dad tried to move back into the house in high school after they'd separated (his apartment had burned down, officially). I said no. I told my sister, who told my mom, who told my brothers without my permission. None of my brothers reached out about it in any way that was memorable. My mom cried and asked why I hadn't said something sooner, said she would've put him in jail — but then, when I described what he specifically did (anal), she said "oh God, that's literally what he does to me too when we do whatever we do." That confirmed she already knew.
    • The more I sit with all of this, the more I think my neglect wasn't ordinary neglect — I don't think most people were neglected the way I was. I can see the same root cause playing out in my brothers and in my sister: my mom consistently prioritizing the men in her life over her own kids.
    • Another example of that pattern: when I was pregnant with my son, still living at my mom's, I spent a lot of time at my partner's place nearby — which seems like a normal thing to want while pregnant with your first child. My mom used that as the excuse to move my dad back into the house, framing it as his apartment burning down, when really it was because he was helping her pay rent.
    • She'd had me paying rent and bills since before I was even 18 — I used to leave high school classes early to work at Shake Shack so I could cover rent. I couldn't go to college, even though I wanted to, because she needed that income from me.
    • After she moved him back in, she called me while I was at my boyfriend's house to tell me my dad was back. I asked her why she'd do that and started bawling. I told my partner (boyfriend at the time) what happened, and he asked his parents if I could stay with them — he barely even had to explain the full situation, and they took me in. That's when I left my mom's house for good.

    My mom has jeopardized my safety my entire life, over and over. I'm genuinely trying to understand how I'm still alive and made it this far with no real help.

    • One more thing before sleep, this morning: my partner has always let me choose — what we eat, what we drink, little everyday things. I used to think it was just him being easygoing. I realized tonight it's actually been him showing me, consistently, that I'm safe with him. That realization brought me to tears.

    • We do have sex, but only if I'm the one initiating or on top. I like my nipples sucked every night; he'll say "I got you" and then just doesn't, unless it happens to occur during sex anyway — which he then counts as having done it. The rules aren't the same for me as they are for him.
    • His idea of foreplay is deflecting my advances — "I'll think about it," acting shy like I'm bothering him. I play into it, but it doesn't turn me on. What actually works for me (like the "mommy" dynamic) only shows up mid-act, like a checkbox, not something he's actually attuned to.
    • Food/portions: he gave me a small portion of liver he made because "I don't eat it all anyway." I just take whatever's shared out — he works, I don't right now, so I don't push for more. The next day he ate all the leftovers without checking with me first; I almost got upset because there was nothing else in the house, he apologized for "being on autopilot," but he'd have finished the food regardless of whether I'd eaten or not. Meanwhile he told me to gain weight and said he could see my collarbone.
    • I know I have an eating disorder — intermittent fasting most days, purging after bingeing as a kid, still sometimes now but not often. I'm working on it, but haven't been treating it as its own named thing until now.
    • Where I landed tonight: I don't think my needs matter unless I make them matter myself. And I'm not sure why I thought leaving my mom meant leaving the neglect behind — it still feels close to home, just relocated into this relationship.
    • The portioning pattern extends beyond food: he rations my weed bowls noticeably smaller than his too — I can see the difference in smoke cloud size when I ask "I packed us the same size bowls, right?" I've also had to directly ask him whether he put the same amount of food on both our plates. It's consistent across more than one kind of portion in the house, not a one-off with the liver.
    • I don't fight for more or push back — I don't care to. I never have to ask people what they need, they just come to me and I help them, and nobody asks why I am the way I am, so I don't say more than necessary, in general — including with movies and videos. Dark content especially hits me as funny rather than disturbing.
    • Expanding on dissociation: I've dissociated for as long as I can remember — during sex, during conversations, all day, constant daydreaming. My thoughts are personified, I talk to myself, always have. I stay functional while dissociating — I can change a diaper fine while dissociated, or cry while taking care of my daughter or doing basically anything, present enough to function but not fully there.

    An old question — why the will to survive, when I had nothing to live for back then

    • I think of myself as metamorphic, not just adaptable — I didn't just cope with each environment, I actually transformed to survive it, repeatedly, while staying myself underneath.
    • I don't know why I had such a strong will to survive as a kid, even though I had nothing to really live for at the time.
    • I watch other women my age or younger and think their spirits look so lightweight. Mine feels very heavy — not in a bad way, in an ancient way.
    • Deep down I don't think many people, maybe nobody, truly empathizes with me. My experiences feel very unique, and I was always alone no matter where I was — St. Vincent, Tortola, the Bronx. The loneliness never left, no matter where I went.
    • My partner is my person, but he's still human, and I'm realizing not everyone is as severely traumatized as I am. I was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder by my APRN after over a year of seeing her, and my therapist at the time came to the same conclusion independently.
    • I also think I might be neurodivergent on top of the BPD diagnosis — want to raise this with Leah directly as its own question, not a replacement theory, especially given the pattern of boys in my family not talking early and my son's own diagnosis.

    Talking points — sharing my research with Leah (verbal only, doc stays mine)

    She knows I'm spiritual and asked me to share what I feel ties into our work. I'm not handing over the document — just talking through it, using it as my own reference.

    • What it is, in one line: a personal research project called "The Root Below the Root" — Roots → Research → Practice → Art — tracing St. Vincent & Tortola heritage, Obeah, and Akan spirituality, paired with a music project called HAIRŪNA (named after "Hairouna," the actual Kalinago name for St. Vincent, meaning "Land of the Blessed").
    • Why it matters here: this is the direct line to my heritage I built specifically to route around my mother as gatekeeper — uncoupling the culture from the person who failed to parent me. It's also where my excitement and my inner world get to live on purpose now, instead of being routed through people who don't meet it.
    • A few specific threads worth mentioning if it comes up: the research into my family's possible connection to African stone-building/metalwork traditions and enslaved skilled trades in Tortola and St. Vincent; the Egungun/Zangbeto ancestral masking traditions; water/ancestor offerings; and the astrological/interpretive layer I've connected to my own natal chart and HAIRŪNA's themes.
    • The secrecy boundary, if it comes up: the historical/academic research (colonial records, named scholars, published sources) is fair to discuss freely — it's public scholarship, not anyone's private knowledge. Anything that would be personal ritual practice or knowledge given to me directly within the tradition stays mine; I can say plainly "that part isn't mine to share" without it being evasive.

    Leah validated the research as part of the work — and what that unlocked

    • I feel blessed to have found such a great therapist. When I told her what I was working on, she said it was a great foundation to have in addition to therapy.
    • This feels like the anchor I was missing — my home away from home.
    • Because I dissociate and get lost in my daydream space, having my ancestors be that anchor literally pulls me back to my roots.
    • Source going back to source — there's true balance in that, true equilibrium.

I need an actual sleep aid — I was taking hydroxyzine as needed, want to discuss adding that or something similar.

    • I've had a recent escalation in anger and self-harm urges, which I'm addressing directly with Leah — flagging it here too since it's relevant to medication decisions and follow-up.
    • A clearer way to name a pattern I keep running into: people won't show up for me in the ways I actually need, but they'll go on social media and "gas me up" publicly — a comment, a like, hyping me up where others can see — as if that's the same as real support. It isn't. Those are two different currencies, and I keep getting paid in the cheap, visible one instead of the real one.
    • Why I didn't engage back with Carl's comment: she still hasn't responded to my last real message — just hearted it instead of actually replying. Her screaming "never" under my post is affirming something I already know about myself (that what's meant for me will come to me) — she's not actually part of that, she's just cheering from outside the club. That's why it doesn't count as real engagement to me.

I have real problems — I'm not sitting in an abusive relationship by my own free will the way she is. She has no obligations tying her to that dynamic and is letting it run her life anyway; that's hers to carry alone. I don't have to be part of it, and I'm not moved by the small, low-effort gestures anymore.

    Luc — sharing my EP, the critiques, and ending the collaboration

    Capturing this while it's fresh because the whole thing rubbed me the wrong way, and I want to understand why.

    • What happened: I put together my 4 songs (beat links, BPMs, lyrics, and a note that the EP is very personal and tied to my ancestor work) and shared it with Luc, a producer I've worked with for over a year, so he could understand the soundscape I'm in. Asking for help has always felt like weakness to me, so sharing it took something. I was also testing whether he could come with me on this next step, and he couldn't.
    • What I got back: he praised the lyrics and the concept of the EP, then moved straight into critique. He said one of my beats (by Stoic) is already famous, so my song would feel like a remix and undermine my originality, warned me about the risk of using samples, and said my vocal melodies and flows sound the same across songs.
    • The flow comment isn't new. He's said it for months, every time I send a new song. When I asked him directly which songs and where, twice, he didn't answer. Looking at my lyrics, each song has a different structure and rhythm, so I can't find what he's describing.
    • What he offered instead: his own beats, or making sample-based beats for me, with credit and a 50/50 split of platform royalties. It felt like being steered toward his sound and his terms instead of hearing what I told him was sacred.
    • My read: he only seems to like my voice, with no critiques, when I'm on his beats (like Bury Me). The vocal cleanup he did was on that song, not my newer ones.
    • How it felt: angry, and stupid for having shown him everything. I don't think he realized how sacred this project is. It felt like he was trying to format me into a white European artist while liking my Afrocentric features, and that felt like colonizing, whether or not he realizes he's doing it.
    • What I did: I sent him a firm message ending the collaboration, told him not to share or use anything I sent, and told him I'm closing the shared folder. I don't want his help anymore.
    • After that: I removed his access to the Dropbox folder without telling him. He then messaged that he was listening and couldn't open the file, and that's why I blocked him. I only shared my songs through that folder, so he didn't get them anywhere else.
    • The pattern I want to look at: every time I open up and show someone my world, I get critiques and instructions for what I should do instead of being met. It connects to Pattern 2 and the 'not being listened to' trigger. It also feeds the thought that people like being in my energy but don't actually like me.
    • Worth exploring with Leah: is ending this with Luc protective, or the same withdraw-when-not-met pattern I described before, and how do I tell the difference? And how do I share something sacred with someone without it feeling like a test they were set up to fail?
    • Moving forward: I'm putting out a call on Instagram for producers who fit the sound I want (70-80 BPM, hypnotic, heavy, sample-heavy, Caribbean and folk-rooted, beats that carry my ancestors) and letting the right people come to me.
    • More detail on why this was protective, not withdrawal: I offered to let him have "Bury Me" and drop it under his own producer Spotify profile. He declined, saying Italy doesn't pay out much on music — then wanted me to open a new ToolOst distribution profile where he'd have access to my account. I declined that too. He'd talk about his own life troubles without ever actually supporting my music, and the moment I pushed back on his vague criticism, he pivoted straight to money. I'm not his meal ticket and I'm not responsible for fixing his life — that shift from artistic critique to financial access the second I didn't comply is what made this read as predatory, not just a difference in taste.
    • Before the EP/money conflict, there was a weird gap: we hadn't talked in a long time. I suggested he see a therapist (referencing him and his partner having each other), mentioning I've been in therapy for years myself. He responded by asking what I'd discovered about myself and said he felt like he was "seeing me in a new light." When I asked him directly what he meant by that, instead of answering, he deflected into heavy, effusive praise — calling me special, my talent "so pure it's hard to find these days." He dodged a direct question with flattery then, the same way he'd later dodge my direct questions about specific songs with vague criticism. Fits a pattern worth naming.
    • Where I'm at generally: I tell people how to move with me in this chapter of my life. If they don't comply, they get cut off. I don't feel bad about it.
    • Earlier screenshots from the Luc thread, now that I've reviewed them: he consistently resisted the simplest, most generous version of any deal (me putting "Bury Me" on his profile as featured artist, no complications) and kept steering toward structures where he'd end up with a standing account/access tie to my work — a "collaborator" account, splits routed through his email, asking what was "holding me back" when I proposed something simpler. He also used oddly intense, intimate language for a producer relationship — "we're so far and so close internally," "it's like a sixth sense," "I tell you with my heart," going on about how strong and special I am. He sent me his own demo and asked if I used autotune to fix myself, which didn't track with the praise.
    • The clearest red flag: I was running the publishing idea by my partner, who got me into music and mixes my songs — he immediately asked why Luc would want that kind of access. I originally offered to let Luc have "Bury Me" under his own profile with me as featured artist because I wasn't confident enough yet to put it on my own artist profile. He didn't want that arrangement. Once I mentioned my partner was involved in the conversation, Luc said "I don't want to cause issues between you two" — which came out of nowhere and didn't fit anything that had actually been said. That reaction told me he'd been relating to this as something closer to personal than professional.
    • I always suspected Luc was flirting with me, but I consistently didn't engage with that — kept redirecting back to it being about the music. My partner trusts me fully. I think I just don't fully register that people are interested in me like that until they start acting weird about it.
    • Update: saw Raquel and told her everything using the notes I prepared. She started me on Trazodone 50mg for sleep.

    What I want to leave session with

    • Ways to regulate myself in the moment that don't depend on my environment or on someone else responding "correctly" — starting with the disappointment-spiral pattern specifically.
    • Language to separate "I am overreacting" from "this is a real and repeated pattern" — I go back and forth between the two and it's hard to trust which one is true in the moment.
    • Help identifying which parts of this are mine to work on regardless of the relationship or friendships, and which parts are patterns in others I shouldn't be trying to self-regulate my way around.
    • Not "am I too much when I'm angry" but: did I ever actually get to practice a middle volume, or did I only ever learn two extremes — whisper/withdrawn and loud enough to hear down the block?
    • Whether isolating myself when I'm angry is protective (I'm managing something well) or corrosive (it's just delaying the same blowup, or making me feel more alone afterward) — those call for pretty different next steps.
    • When did I last let someone see the anger and the vulnerability together, all the way through, without pulling back first — and what actually happened when I did?
    • Whether "I'd have to abandon my whole life to be fulfilled" is actually true, or whether it's a resource-scarcity problem — my current pockets of time are too small and too depleted to hold just existing without a trade-off (sleep, enjoyment). If it's the latter: where, specifically, in a week that's already stretched thin, could there be five or ten protected minutes that are mine without penalty — and what would have to change structurally (help from my partner, a different schedule, saying no to something) to actually protect even that much.
    • Whether "the rules that apply to everyone else don't apply to me" is an accurate read, or whether it's a pattern with specific people (friends, my partner) hardening into a fixed belief about my place with everyone, period — because those call for very different responses.
    • With my partner: matching his disengagement instead of modeling support anymore — is that a fairness boundary (I stop giving what I don't get back, while leaving room for something real to still happen) or a resignation (deciding this is the level we're both at, and quietly settling there)? Worth being clear with myself which one it actually is.
